title: LoDo
name: LoDo
metaDescription: LoDo 1031 exchange guidance for historic warehouse-to-loft conversions, ground-floor retail, and Coors Field-area mixed-use property in downtown Denver.

sections.html: LoDo is short for Lower Downtown, the old warehouse district north of the office towers and hard up against Union Station and Coors Field. Brick-and-timber buildings from the railroad era got converted to lofts, offices, and restaurant space starting in the 1990s, and that conversion is what makes the submarket look nothing like the rest of downtown Denver.

sections.heading: A Landmark District, Not a Blank Lot
sections.html:
Most of LoDo sits inside a designated historic district, and that means Denver Landmark Preservation reviews exterior changes on these buildings, brick repointing, window replacement, signage, all of it. A buyer coming out of a suburban submarket where a facade change is a permit and a Tuesday needs to budget real time for design review here instead.

The upside is the building stock itself. Heavy timber floors, exposed brick, tall ceilings, that construction holds tenant interest in a way a metal-frame 1980s office building never will, and it supports rent premiums for the buildings that have kept their original character intact.

Larimer Square sits at the west edge of LoDo and predates the rest of the district's landmark designation by years, it was the first commercial block in Denver to get historic protection, back in the late 1960s. Buildings there face an even stricter design review process than the broader LoDo district, and a buyer should confirm which specific overlay applies before assuming a renovation scope.

sections.heading: What's on the Identification List in LoDo
sections.html:
The property types that actually show up in this submarket are:

  • historic warehouse buildings converted to office or creative space
  • ground-floor restaurant and bar space fronting Wynkoop, Blake, and Wazee streets
  • loft-style residential conversions above ground-floor retail
  • small boutique retail storefronts serving the Union Station and ballpark crowd

sections.heading: Coors Field and the Game-Day Swing
sections.html:
Coors Field sits on the eastern edge of LoDo, and restaurant and bar revenue in the blocks around it swings hard with the baseball schedule. A tenant's April numbers and a tenant's August numbers can look like two different businesses. Rent-roll analysis on any LoDo restaurant space needs a full season of trailing data, not a snapshot from a strong homestand.

Union Station itself anchors the west side of the district and pulls in commuter rail, Amtrak, and light rail riders who spill into LoDo retail and hospitality on their way to and from work. That foot traffic has kept ground-floor space here leasing better than comparable blocks further from the station.

The station's own renovation, completed in phases through the last decade, turned a working rail terminal into a hotel and dining destination on top of its transit function. Retail space directly inside or adjacent to the station building leases at a real premium over storefronts even a block or two away, and a buyer should treat that inner ring as its own micro-market rather than folding it into a general LoDo average.

sections.heading: Diligence Points That Are Specific to LoDo
sections.html:
Confirm historic district status and any prior alteration approvals before assuming a renovation budget. Check whether a building's structural timber has had a recent engineering review, since deferred maintenance on century-old wood framing is a real cost that doesn't show up on a rent roll. And separate seasonal restaurant income from stable year-round tenants before trusting a cap rate built off peak months.

Basement space in a lot of these older warehouse buildings is a real diligence item too. Moisture intrusion and periodic flood plain concerns near the South Platte River have made some below-grade space unusable for occupied tenant space without a french drain retrofit and a sump system, and that's a cost line a buyer needs quoted before assuming a basement counts as leasable square footage.

sections.heading: Positioning a LoDo Identification
sections.html: Because LoDo buildings tend to be smaller and individually owned rather than large single-tenant packages, most 1031 buyers identify one LoDo property alongside a downtown Denver office asset or a RiNo building as backups. That spread also hedges the seasonal restaurant exposure that comes with a game-day-driven tenant against a steadier office or industrial asset elsewhere in the metro. A qualified intermediary coordinating a LoDo purchase should build in extra time for the closing timeline itself, since title work on a century-old building with a long chain of ownership and prior alteration permits often takes longer to clear than a straightforward suburban parcel with a single prior owner.

faqs.q: Does LoDo's historic district status slow down a purchase?
faqs.a: It affects renovation timelines, not the purchase itself. Budget extra weeks for design review if the plan includes any exterior or facade work on a landmark building.

faqs.q: How much does Coors Field affect restaurant income in LoDo?
faqs.a: A lot. Game-day and homestand months can carry a disproportionate share of annual revenue for bars and restaurants near the ballpark, so a rent roll should be checked against a full twelve-month cycle, not a peak-season snapshot.

faqs.q: Can a LoDo warehouse conversion carry a three-property identification alone?
faqs.a: Rarely, since most individual buildings are smaller assets. Pairing a LoDo property with a downtown Denver or RiNo candidate is the more common approach.

faqs.q: What should a structural review check on an older LoDo building?
faqs.a: Heavy timber framing and brick masonry both need a current engineering opinion, since deferred maintenance on century-old construction is a real line-item cost, not a rounding error.

faqs.q: Is ground-floor retail in LoDo a stable 1031 replacement, or does it turn over fast?
faqs.a: It leans toward faster turnover than suburban net lease, largely restaurants and bars rather than credit tenants. That means shorter lease terms and more turnover cost to underwrite up front.
